(2) The declination of the primary magnetization indicates substantial clockwise rotation within this sector of the Variscan thrust belt. Rotation is most likely to be linked to early Variscan northward thrust transport with components of dextral transpression. The amount of clockwise rotation is approximately 85" in the south (Mendips) and decreases to 33-63" in the north (Tortworth). Such reconstructions are based on the interpretation of regional geologic features and on the extrapolation, both in space and in time, of the palcomagnetic data from the mostly Meso-Cenozoic allochthonous units of the Apennines. In order to investigate the relationships between the opening in the Tyrrhenian sea and the evolution of the Apennines, the neo-autochthonous Plio-Pleistocene clayey sediments of the Central Italy Tyrrhenian margin, that are suitable both for their tectonic position and age, were sampled for palcomagnetic analyses. The studied sector is characterized by the development of important fault-bounded transverse basins, interpreted as Copyright 1994 by the American Geophysical Union. Paper number 94GL00393 0094-8534/94/94GL-00393503.00 major transfer structures in the framework of the overall margin extension. Moreover, strike-slip shear zones in Pleistocene sediments were recently recognized [Faccenna et al., 1993]. These geologic features were investigated as a possible source of block-rotation mechanisms. Geologic Setting The structural setting of the Central Italy Tyrrhenian margin developed in a typical post-oro

"pull-apart\" basins, thermomineral springs, travertine deposition and volcano-tectonic features. Crustal extension in the Central Tyrrhenian margin was accompained by volcanism, with volcanic centers following a NW-SE elongated sinking belt [Locardi et al., 1977]. Volcanic activity in the area started during the Pliocene (acidic series of the Tolfa-Ceriti area), but reached a climax in Middle-Upper Pleistocene with the onset of the huge volcanic complexes (high- potassium series) of the Roman Comagmatic Province. Sampling and Measurements Sampling was performed by in situ drilling using a diamond- head corer, cooled by water. 22 sites (Figure 1) were sampled in the grey-blue coloured fine-grained marine marly-clayey units, from different structural settings in the Tyrrhenian margin around Rome. The stratigraphic ages of the sampled units range from Upper Miocene (Messinian (6.5 - 5 Ma); sites LZ16 - Z17) to Lower Pleistocene (Emilian (1.4 - 1.1 Ma); site LZ02). A Gondwanan origin is commonly assumed for this belt, but a “Laurasian” origin for the Chitral region has been argued on palaeontological (Talent and Mawson, 1979) and palaeomagnetic (Klootwijk and Conaghan, 1979) grounds. The “Laurasian” view was based on a pilot study we undertook of Upper Devonian pisolitic ironstones from a thrust sheet at Kuragh Spur in Chitral. Preliminary results showed a characteristic magnetization component [II = 318”, I = - 6.5”, N = 7 (block samples), k = 14, aq5 = 16.5”] indicating an equatorial palaeoposition. This component was thought to be of primary origin and was interpreted in terms of a Late Devonian “Laurasian” affinity of the Kursgh Spur rocks. This controversial conclusion has been tested in the present more comprehensive study of the thrust pile of sedimentary rocks in the ReshIin-Kurlgh-Bikini region of Chitral and the primary origin of the characteristic magnetization component refuted. Thermal demagnetization of 333 block samples from Middle to Upper Devonian variegated sediments, Permian quartz flysch, Permo-Triassic carbonates, and mid-Cretaceous redbeds showed two interpretable components. A softer component of recent origin (A); and a harder characteristic component (B) of both normal and reverse polarity whose mean direction [L) = 314.1”, I = 6.0”, N = 4 (thrust sheets), k = 198.2, aas = 6.5”] is comparable to the characteristic component observed in our preliminary study. However, the universal presence of this component throughout the thrust pile proves its overprint origin, which we attribute to initial India-Asia contact. Palaeomag- netic information pertinent to the controversy of a “Laurasian” versus a Gondwanan origin of the Chitral region has not been obtained in this further study because primary magnetizations could not be identified beyond doubt. Hence, we retract herewith our original conclusion of a Late Devonian “Laurasian” affinity of the Chitral region on the basis of the palaeomagnetic evidence. Introduction This study is a follow-up to a palaeomagnetic reconnaissance (Klootwijk and Conaghan, 1979) of Upper Devonian sedimentary ironstones from Chitral (Pakistan) in the Eastern Hindukush. The results of the earlier study of a limited collection of sedimentary ironstones showed a characteristic magnetization component that we interpreted as having been primary and indicative of an equato- rial palaeolatitude. Comparison with the then available palaeomagnetic data from “Laurasia” and Gondwana together with palaeontological ar- guments (Talent and Mawson, 1979) led us to conclude that the Chitral region is an original part of Asia and does not have Gondwanan affin- ity, but also that the Eastern Hindukush under- went large-scale counterclockwise rotation and northward displacement relative to the Siberian platform as a result of India’s penetration into southern Asia during the Cainozoic. section_candidates.excerpt: 18 January 1994; revision accepted 24 May 1994 Abstract The Eastern Hindukush forms part of an elongate belt (“Central Domain”, collage of Cimmerian microconti- nents) that encircles the northern part of the Indian subcontinent. A Gondwanan origin is commonly assumed for this belt, but a “Laurasian” origin for the Chitral region has been argued on palaeontological (Talent and Mawson, 1979) and palaeomagnetic (Klootwijk and Conaghan, 1979) grounds. The “Laurasian” view was based on a pilot study we undertook of Upper Devonian pisolitic ironstones from a thrust sheet at Kuragh Spur in Chitral. Preliminary results showed a characteristic magnetization component [II = 318”, I = - 6.5”, N = 7 (block samples), k = 14, aq5 = 16.5”] indicating an equatorial palaeoposition. This component was thought to be of primary origin and was interpreted in terms of a Late Devonian “Laurasian” affinity of the Kursgh Spur rocks. This controversial conclusion has been tested in the present more comprehensive study of the thrust pile of sedimentary rocks in the ReshIin-Kurlgh-Bikini region of Chitral and the primary origin of the characteristic magnetization component refuted. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: al setting and timing of deformation in the Southeast Pyrenees The Pedraforca Unit can be subdivided into an upper and a lower thrust sheet based on its Cretaceous stratigraphy (Verges and Martinez, 1988). The upper Pedraforca thrust sheet is domi- nated by Early Cretaceous limestone. By contrast, the lower thrust sheet is mainly built up by the Bona Formation, a thick sequence of Late Creta- ceous shelf limestone (Mey et al., 1968). During the latest Cretaceous and the earliest Tertiary the upper thrust sheet was emplaced onto the Bona Formation (Ullastre et al., 1987). During the Early Eocene, the two thrust sheets of the Pedraforca Unit were emplaced onto the Paleogene Pyre- nean foreland, whereas the upper thrust sheet was passively transported, riding on the lower one (Verges and Martinez, 1988). At Aigua de Valls (Fig. 2) the end of this tectonic phase can be dated as Lutetian by flysch sediments overlying an erosional discordance (horizon A in Fig. 2; Sole-Sugrafies, 1972). Subsequent N-S compression led to deforma- tion of the Paleogene foreland (Puigdefabregas et S Sierra de Busa Aigua de Valls Montcalb N Fig. 2. Shortening during middle and Late Oligocene led to folds and thrusts in the Ebro Basin (Verges et al., 1992). The Sanaiija and Suria anticlines mark the southern front of this deformation (Fig. lb), and are the youngest struc- tures related to Pyrenean thrust tectonics. At Montcalb the conglomerates of the Berga Formation cover an erosional horizon on the Cadi Unit (horizon B in Fig. 2). Masriera and Ullastre (1985) dated this erosion as younger than late Bartonian. To the north the erosional hori- zon can be followed onto the Pedraforca Unit (Fig. 1 b). The conglomerates of the Berga Forma- tion seal the tectonic contact between the two units. In the Pedraforca Unit the conglomerates are often folded (Keller and Gehring, 1992) or overthrust by Mesozoic sediments (GuCrin-De- sjardins and Latreille, 1961). In the northern part of the Pedraforca Unit, strike-slip faults dissect the post-Bartonian conglomerates as well as the thrust structures (Fig. lb; Sole-Sugrafies, 1973; Ullastre et al., 1987; Durand-Delga et al., 1989). The upper Pedraforca thrust sheet is domi- nated by Early Cretaceous limestone. By contrast, the lower thrust sheet is mainly built up by the Bona Formation, a thick sequence of Late Creta- ceous shelf limestone (Mey et al., 1968). During the latest Cretaceous and the earliest Tertiary the upper thrust sheet was emplaced onto the Bona Formation (Ullastre et al., 1987). During the Early Eocene, the two thrust sheets of the Pedraforca Unit were emplaced onto the Paleogene Pyre- nean foreland, whereas the upper thrust sheet was passively transported, riding on the lower one (Verges and Martinez, 1988). The other model, however, challenged thin-skinned thrust- ing of the Cadi Unit, and explains the contact between the two units of the Southeast Pyrenees by means of Neogene wrench tectonics (Durand- Delga et al., 19891, which formed the steep Cadi and Vallfogona faults (Fig. 1). If the Cadi Unit is autochthonous then the amount of shortening in the East Pyrenees has to be less than that pro- posed in the thrust model. Palaeomagnetic data from the Pyrenean fore- land (Dinares et al., 1992) and the Pedraforca Unit (Keller and Gehring, 1992) have shown con- trasting rotation of single anticlines, which can be interpreted by tectonic rotation about vertical axes. None of the above models (i.e., thrust tec- tonics vs. wrench tectonics) has considered these rotations. The aim of this study is to present regionally distributed palaeomagnetic data, in or- der to develop a deformation scenario for the Southeast Pyrenees that includes tectonic rota- tion. 2. Characteristic remanent magnetization directions have been isolated after detailed thermal demagnetization for sixteen sites. The spatial and temporal characteristics of arc magmatism and crustal de- formation have been investigated in an attempt to understand the kinematics and dynamics of plate tectonic evolution. For western Mexico, this has not been an easy task and even the present-day plate tectonic boundaries and motions are not fully documented (Minster and Jordan, 1979; Klitgord and Mam- merickx, 1982; Eissler and McNally, 1984; John- son and Harrison, 1990; Bandy, 1992). These young foredeep sediments of the eastern part of the Bradano Unit and the underlying Mesozoic-early Tertiary carbonate sequence are affected by some minor normal faulting (Cristo- folini et al., 1985). Our previous paleomagnetic study of Early Pleis- tocene clays from the Matera region showed a counter-clockwise rotation over approximately 23” for the southeastern part of the southern Apen- nines Fold Belt (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1993). This rotation is thought to have occurred during the middle Pleistocene, between 1.0 and 0.7 Ma, and is most probably connected to a middle Pleis- tocene compressive phase. We also found tec- tonic rotations in the opposite sense (15’ clock- wise) during the middle Pleistocene for the Cal- abro-Peloritan block (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1994) which is situated to the south of the south- ern Apennines fold-and-thrust belt (Fig. 1). Pale- omagnetic data of Cretaceous rocks from the southern Apenninic belt also imply counter- clockwise rotations (Channel1 and Tarling, 1975; Catalan0 et al., 1976; Incoronato, 1983; Jackson, 1990). Paleomagnetic results from the sites in the internal part (more western) of the southern Apenninic belt show a larger counter-clockwise rotation (89“) than the sites from the more exter- nal (eastern) part. Our previous paleomagnetic study of Early Pleis- tocene clays from the Matera region showed a counter-clockwise rotation over approximately 23” for the southeastern part of the southern Apen- nines Fold Belt (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1993). This rotation is thought to have occurred during the middle Pleistocene, between 1.0 and 0.7 Ma, and is most probably connected to a middle Pleis- tocene compressive phase. We also found tec- tonic rotations in the opposite sense (15’ clock- wise) during the middle Pleistocene for the Cal- abro-Peloritan block (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1994) which is situated to the south of the south- ern Apennines fold-and-thrust belt (Fig. 1). Pale- omagnetic data of Cretaceous rocks from the southern Apenninic belt also imply counter- clockwise rotations (Channel1 and Tarling, 1975; Catalan0 et al., 1976; Incoronato, 1983; Jackson, 1990). Paleomagnetic results from the sites in the internal part (more western) of the southern Apenninic belt show a larger counter-clockwise rotation (89“) than the sites from the more exter- nal (eastern) part. We sampled different parts of the tectonic system: sites from both the internal (western) and the external (eastern) part. The characteristic remanent magnetisation (ChRM) component for the sediments is generally removed from 320-340” up to 450-480°C. A counter-clockwise rotation is observed for nearly all sites. All data indicate that the main tectonic rotations in the southern Apennines fold-and-thrust belt occurred in the middle Pleistocene. The Apulian Unit extends to the west, struc- turally below the deposits of the Bradano Unit (Fig. 11, a succession of marine clays that was accumulated in a Plio-Pleistocene foredeep. These young foredeep sediments of the eastern part of the Bradano Unit and the underlying Mesozoic-early Tertiary carbonate sequence are affected by some minor normal faulting (Cristo- folini et al., 1985). Our previous paleomagnetic study of Early Pleis- tocene clays from the Matera region showed a counter-clockwise rotation over approximately 23” for the southeastern part of the southern Apen- nines Fold Belt (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1993). This rotation is thought to have occurred during the middle Pleistocene, between 1.0 and 0.7 Ma, and is most probably connected to a middle Pleis- tocene compressive phase. We also found tec- tonic rotations in the opposite sense (15’ clock- wise) during the middle Pleistocene for the Cal- abro-Peloritan block (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1994) which is situated to the south of the south- ern Apennines fold-and-thrust belt (Fig. 1). Pale- omagnetic data of Cretaceous rocks from the southern Apenninic belt also imply counter- clockwise rotations (Channel1 and Tarling, 1975; Catalan0 et al., 1976; Incoronato, 1983; Jackson, 1990). Paleomagnetic results from the sites in the internal part (more western) of the southern Apenninic belt show a larger counter-clockwise rotation (89“) than the sites from the more exter- nal (eastern) part. Our previous paleomagnetic study of Early Pleis- tocene clays from the Matera region showed a counter-clockwise rotation over approximately 23” for the southeastern part of the southern Apen- nines Fold Belt (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1993). This rotation is thought to have occurred during the middle Pleistocene, between 1.0 and 0.7 Ma, and is most probably connected to a middle Pleis- tocene compressive phase. We also found tec- tonic rotations in the opposite sense (15’ clock- wise) during the middle Pleistocene for the Cal- abro-Peloritan block (Fig. 1; Scheepers et al., 1994) which is situated to the south of the south- ern Apennines fold-and-thrust belt (Fig. 1). Pale- omagnetic data of Cretaceous rocks from the southern Apenninic belt also imply counter- clockwise rotations (Channel1 and Tarling, 1975; Catalan0 et al., 1976; Incoronato, 1983; Jackson, 1990). On its southeast side is the 1854 + 11Ma Wathaman batholith that marks the suture zone for the juvenile terranes of the Trans-Hudson orogen (THO), and on its northwest side is the Wollaston fold belt that defines the margin of the Archean Slave-Rae- Hearne (SRH) craton. Two well-defined remanent magnetization components are carried by hematite, magnetite and pyrrhotite in a range of metamorphic rock types. The A component was probably acquired during the D 1 regional metamorphic event at ~ 1869 Ma and gives a direction ofD = 302 °, I= - 40 ° (o/95 = 10 o, k= 16, N= 15 ). More significantly it is the main com- ponent in three of five sites in the Parker Lake mafic gneisses. The B component is easily defined by AF de- magnetization although the contribution of vis- cous remanent magnetization (VRM) from the present Earth's magnetic field (PEMF) to B in a given specimen is not easily estimated as they are about parallel in direction (Figs. 3b, 6a, 6b). Experimental methods The Peter Lake domain was sampled at 28 sites along the Highway 105 transect and the shore- line of Peter Lake (Fig. 2). Of these sites, twenty are in the metagabbros and three in the monzon- ites of the Peter Lake complex. The remaining five sites are in the Parker Lake mafic gneisses to provide paleomagnetic contact tests between the Wathaman batholith and the Peter Lake do- main, and between the gneisses and the complex in the domain. Five cores were drilled at most sites and ori- ented in situ by sun compass. Two specimens were later sliced from most cores to yield a total collection of 259 specimens. All measurements were done inside a shielded room. The speci- mens' natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) were measured using an automated CTF DRM- 420 cryogenic magnetometer. Summary The metamorphosed gabbro-monzonite rock suite of the Peter Lake complex retains a com- mon A ChRM direction in magnetic domains with unblocking temperatures ranging from about 300 to 700°C. The A component predates intrusion of the adjacent massive 1854+ 11 Ma Wathaman batholith, and correlates most evi- dently with the D 1 regional metamorphic event in the Peter Lake domain. The best estimate for the age of the D 1 event and of the A component is 1869 + 29 Ma based on scant radiometric data, but it is unlikely to be older than the onset of the Hudsonian orogeny at about 1900 Ma. The A pole agrees with the coeval SRH pole in paleoin- clination showing that the Peter Lake domain was beside the SRH craton at about 1870 Ma, but disagrees in paleodeclination showing that the domain was rotated 32 ° _+ 14 ° counterclockwise relative to the craton after about 1870 Ma. It is separated on its northwestern side from the Wollaston fold belt of the SRH craton by the Needle Falls shear zone, and on its southeastern side from the Wathaman batholith by the Parker Lake shear zone. Both zones are en P.chelon ductile mylonitic shears with dextral strike-slip displacements (LewD, and Collerson, 1990). The domain is comprised of medium- to coarse-grained plutonic rocks of dioritic to gabbroic composition with minor me- tapyroxenite and anorthosite that have been in- truded by granitic rocks ranging from monzonite to alaskite in composition (Lewry et al., 1980). In the study area (Fig. 2), the mafic rocks are mostly weakly foliated gabbros, metagabbros and amphibolites, and the granitic rocks are quartz- bearing monzonites to biotite monzogranite. Experimental methods The Peter Lake domain was sampled at 28 sites along the Highway 105 transect and the shore- line of Peter Lake (Fig. 2). Of these sites, twenty are in the metagabbros and three in the monzon- ites of the Peter Lake complex. The remaining five sites are in the Parker Lake mafic gneisses to provide paleomagnetic contact tests between the Wathaman batholith and the Peter Lake do- main, and between the gneisses and the complex in the domain. Five cores were drilled at most sites and ori- ented in situ by sun compass. Two specimens were later sliced from most cores to yield a total collection of 259 specimens. All measurements were done inside a shielded room. The speci- mens' natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) were measured using an automated CTF DRM- 420 cryogenic magnetometer. This pole falls on the 1650 Ma position of the Irving ( 1979 ) apparent polar wander path (APWP). Summary The metamorphosed gabbro-monzonite rock suite of the Peter Lake complex retains a com- mon A ChRM direction in magnetic domains with unblocking temperatures ranging from about 300 to 700°C. The A component predates intrusion of the adjacent massive 1854+ 11 Ma Wathaman batholith, and correlates most evi- dently with the D 1 regional metamorphic event in the Peter Lake domain. The best estimate for the age of the D 1 event and of the A component is 1869 + 29 Ma based on scant radiometric data, but it is unlikely to be older than the onset of the Hudsonian orogeny at about 1900 Ma. The A pole agrees with the coeval SRH pole in paleoin- clination showing that the Peter Lake domain was beside the SRH craton at about 1870 Ma, but disagrees in paleodeclination showing that the domain was rotated 32 ° _+ 14 ° counterclockwise relative to the craton after about 1870 Ma. Dex- tral strike-slip kinematic indicators on the do- main-bounding Needle Falls and Parker Lake shear zones argue strongly against either some 3000 km of left-lateral transcurrent fault motion or simple domain rotation about a vertical axis to explain the discordance of the poles. It is separated on its northwestern side from the Wollaston fold belt of the SRH craton by the Needle Falls shear zone, and on its southeastern side from the Wathaman batholith by the Parker Lake shear zone. Fur- thermore, samples from the Isokivennokka gran- ite did not give reliable palaeomagnetic results. Hence, plate tectonic interpretations of the Kola suture belt could not be tested with palaeomag- netic data. Palaeomagnetic investigations were carded out on the Tsuomasvard layered ultramafic intru- sion and the surrounding gabbro-diorite intru- sion (Fig. 3 ), because they proved to carry mul- ticomponent remanent magnetizations (Mertanen and Pesonen, 1992 ). It is important to isolate the different magnetizations, because they can have been formed in several thermal, chemical or hydrothermal processes and may thus reflect the complex geological evolution of the northern Fennoscandian shield. The aim of this paper is to study the nature and origin of these magnetizations. We have attempted to as- sociate the magnetizations with geologic events in the northern Fennoscandian shield by dating them, using isotopic age determinations and by comparing pole positions with poles of previous studies from Fennoscandia. 2. ic study. On geological grounds it was suggested that the Tsuomasvarri ultramafic in- trusion was Palaeoproterozoic in age ( ~ 2.4 Ga) (R. Kesola, pers. commun., 1986). The Ar- chaean Isokivennokka granite ( ~ 2.6 Ga) (Fig. 2 ) was chosen to represent the northeastern side of the Kola suture. Later, however, new isotopic age determinations (M. Vaasjoki, in Forsberg- Heikkil~i, 1989) showed that the gabbro-diorite is as young as of Svecokarelian age (1.93 Ga) and since it cuts the ultramafic intrusion, the ul- tramafic intrusion is younger than 1.93 Ga. Fur- thermore, samples from the Isokivennokka gran- ite did not give reliable palaeomagnetic results. cedure The Tsuomasvarri intrusions form a well-ex- posed 435 m high hill. Fifty-five oriented core samples were taken from ten sites in the ultra- marie intrusion (Fig. 3), using the techniques described previously in Mertanen et al. ( 1987 ). Pesonen Laboratory for Palaeomagnetism, Geological Survey of Finland, SF-02150 Espoo, Finland Received June 22, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994 Abstract Preliminary palaeomagnetic results are presented for the Proterozoic Tsuomasvarri central ultramafic intrusion and surrounding, older gabbro-diorite intrusion in the northeastern Fennoscandian shield. In the ultramafic intru- sion, five remanence components, reflecting different geological processes, were isolated in the alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization of 55 samples from ten sites. A reversed polarity remanence component C (pole: Plat = 26 °N, Plon = 245 ° E, dp= 5 °, dm = 9 °, n = 32 samples) dominates in the ultramafic intrusion. The normal polarity pole A (Plat=44°N, Plon=232°E, dp=4 °, din=6 °, n=9 samples) corresponds to an age of ~ 1.88 Ga on the Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP), and is probably a thermochemical remanence acquired during the Svecokarelian orogeny or in the late stages of magma cooling. cedure The Tsuomasvarri intrusions form a well-ex- posed 435 m high hill. Fifty-five oriented core samples were taken from ten sites in the ultra- marie intrusion (Fig. 3), using the techniques described previously in Mertanen et al. ( 1987 ). The majority of the samples (45) are olivine py- roxenites, six are serpentinite dunites and four are hornblendites (see Fig. 3). In the surround- ing gabbro-diorite 46 samples were taken from ten sites (Fig. 3 ). The NRM was measured on spinner magne- tometers (Pesonen et al., 1983). AF demagneti- zations were done with a single-axis demagne- tizer (in steps of 10 mT, up to 100 mT), and thermal demagnetization was performed (in steps of 100°C up to 500°C and then in 20-10°C steps up to 680 °C ) in Schonstedt or homemade furnaces (Leino, 1979; Pesonen et al., 1983). Susceptibilities were measured in the course of thermal demagnetizations (in steps of 200°C, 300°C, 400°C, 500°C, 520°C, 570°C, 600°C, 640°C and 680°C) to detect mineralogical changes, interpreted on the basis of changes in bulk susceptibility during heating. Magnetiza- tions were isolated using principal component analyses (Kirschvink, 1980) with maximum an- gular deviation (MAD) values of 6 ° in most samples and up to 10 ° in some cases with larger scatter. Probably due to the dif- fering abilities of the rocks to resist remagneti- zations, some magnetizations are encountered only sporadically throughout the various sites. Usually one specimen carries one or two differ- ent components and the components vary from specimen to specimen. In addition, most sam- ples reveal a large component of the present Earth's field (PEF) magnetization which also diminishes the number of accepted samples. For this reason the number of samples used in the analysis is unfortunately fairly low for obtaining statistically well defned means. However, we re- port the results of these investigations, knowing that the interpretations are based on limited data. For the Tsuomasvarri ultramafic intrusion, we have separated five remanence components (hereafter called A, B, C, D and F) all of which we believe to have geological significance. The ultramafic intrusion is dominated by a well- grouped southeasterly and moderate upward magnetization, C. Vaasjoki, in Forsberg- Heikkil~i, 1989) showed that the gabbro-diorite is as young as of Svecokarelian age (1.93 Ga) and since it cuts the ultramafic intrusion, the ul- tramafic intrusion is younger than 1.93 Ga. Fur- thermore, samples from the Isokivennokka gran- ite did not give reliable palaeomagnetic results. Hence, plate tectonic interpretations of the Kola suture belt could not be tested with palaeomag- netic data. Palaeomagnetic investigations were carded out on the Tsuomasvard layered ultramafic intru- sion and the surrounding gabbro-diorite intru- sion (Fig. 3 ), because they proved to carry mul- ticomponent remanent magnetizations (Mertanen and Pesonen, 1992 ). It is important to isolate the different magnetizations, because they can have been formed in several thermal, chemical or hydrothermal processes and may thus reflect the complex geological evolution of the northern Fennoscandian shield. The aim of this paper is to study the nature and origin of these magnetizations. We have attempted to as- sociate the magnetizations with geologic events in the northern Fennoscandian shield by dating them, using isotopic age determinations and by comparing pole positions with poles of previous studies from Fennoscandia. 2. Sampling and measurement Samples were collected from all formations of the Vadsz Group with the exception of the Pad- deby Formation. In the Barents Sea Group, the Kongsfjord, B~sn~ring and B/ttstjord Forma- tions were sampled. Only hand-samples were collected. In-situ orientation of the samples was made with magnetic and sun compasses. From each sample up to five specimens were drilled and cut for measurements. Measurements were made on Geofyzika JR-3 and JR-5 and on Digico and Molspin fluxgate spinner magnetometers. Con- ventional stepwise alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization techniques were used for isolating the characteristic magnetic compo- nents. Chemical demagnetization was made us- ing 8 N hydrochloric acid. Holes were drilled in the samples to facilitate the penetration of the acid. The solution time was up to 1800 hours. Introduction The Neoproterozoic (Late Riphean and Ven- dian) period of the Earth's history involved the formation and split of large landmasses. Re- cently, new ideas about the ancient configura- tion of these blocks have emerged (e.g. Hoff- man, 1991) and palaeomagnetism is an important method for tracing these movements. However, palaeomagnetic data are scarce for this time period, particularly for the Fennoscandian Shield. The rock units available on the Shield are sedimentary successions within and along the eastern margin of the Scandinavian Caledon- ides, often affected by this orogeny and the Late Riphean-Early Vend

three units, in ascending order: the Vads~ Group, the Tan- afjord Group and the Vestertana Group. These units are separated from the allochthonous rock succession in the Barents Sea Region in the north by the Trollt]ord-Komagelv Fault (Johnson et al., 1978). Furthermore, the Caledonian Front with the Kalak Nappe Complex covers the northwest- ern corner of the peninsula (Fig. 1 ). Re- cently, new ideas about the ancient configura- tion of these blocks have emerged (e.g. Hoff- man, 1991) and palaeomagnetism is an important method for tracing these movements. However, palaeomagnetic data are scarce for this time period, particularly for the Fennoscandian Shield. Intrusive age relationships suggest an age >12850 Ma although direct attempts at dating the Nyanzian have pro- duced disparate results. Our study involves a suite of samples collected from the Nyanzian basalts, pillow basalts, andesites and rhyolites from sixteen sites in western Kenya. These rocks yield a tilt-corrected paleomagnetic pole at 14 o N, 150 °E (K= 59, dp = 5 °, dm = 7 ° ). This pole is constrained to be older than the first (D 1

(1984) considered this age to represent a younger limit to the Dodoman metamorphism. The Nyanzian System consists of a succession composed of, from top to bottom: a greywacke and andesitic volcanic group with abundant banded iron formations; an intermediate group composed of rhyolites with intercalated tufts and agglomerates and a basal unit composed of marie volcanic rocks (pillow lavas and flows) with some (rare)banded ironstones (Shackleton, 1946). The total thickness of the Nyanzian Sys- tem has been estimated at 7500 m (Grantham, 1945). The Kavirondian System unconformably ov- erlies the Nyanzian rocks and is composed of pelitic rocks, arkoses and conglomerates. Nei- ther the Kavirondian nor the Nyanzian Systems are well-dated; in fact, the published ages for the Nyanzian rocks were reported by Yanagi and Suwa (1981) as 2710+340 Ma (Rb-Sr whole rock) and 2380 + 250 Ma (Rb-Sr, Bell and Dod- son, 1981 ). These ages only roughly overlap and the large errors associated with the ages suggest that neither can be considered reliable. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: ed August, 1992 Abstract The Nyanzian System lavas of western Kenya are believed to be the oldest rocks of the Tanzanian Craton. Intrusive age relationships suggest an age >12850 Ma although direct attempts at dating the Nyanzian have pro- duced disparate results. Our study involves a suite of samples collected from the Nyanzian basalts, pillow basalts, andesites and rhyolites from sixteen sites in western Kenya. These rocks yield a tilt-corrected paleomagnetic pole at 14 o N, 150 °E (K= 59, dp = 5 °, dm = 7 ° ). This pole is constrained to be older than the first (D 1 ) deformation ( > 2472 + 30 Ma) by positive fold, conglomerate and reversal tests. Analysis of the paleomagnetic data base for three African cratonic nuclei (Tanzanian, Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe and West Africa) for the time period from 2.0 Ga to 3.0 Ga demonstrates a paucity of well-dated poles, although there are several poles from the Kaapvaal/Zim- babwe and Tanzanian Cratons which allow "spot-readings" of their relative positions. We demonstrate, based on these data, that the Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe and Tanzanian Cratons were drifting independently at ~ 2875 Ma, ~ 2700 Ma and ~ 2450 Ma. This independent motion of the Tanzanian and Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe Cratons indicates that previously proposed models involving African cratonic

e Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe and Tanzanian Cratons were drifting independently at ~ 2875 Ma, ~ 2700 Ma and ~ 2450 Ma. This independent motion of the Tanzanian and Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe Cratons indicates that previously proposed models involving African cratonic coherence can no longer be considered valid for the time period from 2850 to 2500 Ma. I. Introduction One of the salient problems in modern geology remains the characterization of Archean and Pa- leoproterozoic tectonics. The nature and style of tectonism during the Earth's infancy may one day be elucidated by a set of high-quality paleomag- netic data. Defining Archean-Paleoproterozoic apparent polar wander paths is difficult given the paucity of data from different continents; how- * Present address: Department of Geography and Geology, Indiana State University, Terre Haute, IN 47809, USA, Fax 812-237-8029. ever, recent works by Symons ( 1991 ) and Hale (1991 ) have demonstrated the efficacy of ap- proaching the problem on a smaller scale (i.e. motions between individual nuclei). In addi- tion, questions regarding the exact nature of the Earth's early magnetic field may be revealed through paleomagnetic investigations (e.g. na- ture of reversals). These belts effectively isolate the Tanzanian Craton from other Archean nu- clei that constitute the larger Congo Craton (Fig. 1 b). The Tanzanian Craton is composed of gran- itic rocks, schist belts, greenstone belts and younger cover rocks. A knowledge of the remanent magnetization, the magnetic suscepti- bility and the anisotropy of magnetic suscepti- bility (AMS) of banded-iron formations (BIFs) and iron ores of the Hamersley Group was re- quired to assist in exploration. Dales Gorge Member and the Joffre Member), the Weeli Wolli Formation and the Boolgeeda Iron Formation. The Wittenoom Dolomite occurs between the lowest two BIFs. The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The myriad of mineralogical and textural va- rieties present in the ores has been studied in de- tail by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ). The following brief summary of current ideas on the BIF to ore transformation is far from comprehensive and only serves to give the reader a flavour of the complex evolution recognized by Morris. Fol- lowing exposure of fresh BIF during a period of uplift and erosion, iron has been concentrated at depth by an electrochemical supergene process. This involved concentration by leaching of some gangue without replacement, as well as the me- tasomatic replacement of gangue (chert and car- bonates) by hydrous iron oxides, mostly goe- thite. Magnetite in the fresh BIF is converted to martite and cation-deficient magnetite, termed "kenomagnetite" by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ), during the ore-forming process. Anisotropy also causes cones of confidence to be underestimated, due to compression of the range of inclinations. In principle, deflection of post-folding remanence towards the bedding plane by high magnetic anisotropy can produce an ap- parent syn-folding signature, with best agreement between directions from different fold limbs after partial unfold- ing. Thus high anisotropy cannot only bias estimated palaeofield directions and cause underestimation of errors, but can also mislead interpretation of the time of remanence acquisition. The anisotropy of anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) probably yields an upper limit to the anisotropy of the chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) carried by the BIFs. Therefore, from the anisotropy of ARM, a maximum inclination deflection of 9 ° is suggested for the sampled BIFs. This corresponds to less than 5 ° change of palaeolatitude. The palaeomagnetic pole position calculated for BIFs at Paraburdoo is 40.9 ° S, 225.0 °E (dp = 2.9 °, drn = 5.8 ° ) after tilt correction, but without correction for anisotropy. Other pole positions reported include that from fiat- lying BIFs from Wittenoom at 36.4 ° S, 218.9 ° E (dp = 4.6 °, dm= 9.1 ° ), from Mount Tom Price iron ore at 37.4 ° S, 220.3°E (dp= 5.7 °, din= 11.3 ° ) and from Paraburdoo ore at 36.4 ° S, 209.9°E (dp= 4.7 °, din= 8.8 ° ). The Hamersley and Fortescue Groups were subjected to low-grade (lowermost prehnite- pumpellyite facies to lowermost greenschist fa- cies) metamorphism due to burial beneath >t 5 km of the Turee Creek Group (Smith et al., 1982), before the initial folding, uplift and par- tial erosion of the Mount Bruce Supergroup. Metamorphic temperatures in the Hamersley Group nowhere exceeded ~ 300 °C and are often considerably lower. A slightly lower grade of bur- ial metamorphism at Paraburdoo is associated with relict primary haematite overgrown by magnetite in the BIFs, whereas elsewhere, e.g. at Mount Tom Price and Wittenoom, the meta- morphic grade is higher and replacement of pri- mary haematite by magnetite is essentially com- plete (Morris, 1985 ). This is evidence that most of the magnetite in the BIFs was produced dur- ing the burial metamorphism. Klein ( 1983 ) has discussed diagenesis and metamorphism of BIF, including the generation of magnetite as a late diagenetic/low-grade metamorphic mineral. It has been suggested that the change from the "anoxic" conditions conducive to BIF forma- tion, to those favouring supergene iron enrich- ment, was related to the oxygen content of the Precambrian atmosphere reaching a threshold level able to satisfy the various oxygen "sinks" (Cloud, 1983 ). In some areas, combined AF and thermal demagnetiza- tion has been shown to be very effective when dealing with rocks whose remanences have been disturbed by relatively strong magnetic fields ( > 5 mT) such as those accompanying lightning strikes (Schmidt and Embleton, 1985). Al- though this approach was adopted here as a rou- tine procedure for treating samples collected from natural outcrop, samples from natural outcrops often yielded scattered remanence directions after treatment. The remaining outcrop samples appear to have escaped significant IRM overprinting and their NRM directions may be regarded as representa- tive of oxidized BIF. Moderate weathering of BIF should reduce both the susceptibility and reman- ence as magnetite alters to haematite. However, remanence direction should remain unchanged as long as even a small fraction of unoxidized magnetite remains to dominate the NRM. Even- tually, complete oxidation of the magnetite should produce weak NRMs similar to those of Tertiary laterites with scattered normal and re- versed groups, plus many intermediate direc- tions (see Schmidt and Embleton, 1976; Idnurm and Senior, 1978; Idnurm and Schmidt, 1986). 5.2. The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The Hamersley and Fortescue Groups were subjected to low-grade (lowermost prehnite- pumpellyite facies to lowermost greenschist fa- cies) metamorphism due to burial beneath >t 5 km of the Turee Creek Group (Smith et al., 1982), before the initial folding, uplift and par- tial erosion of the Mount Bruce Supergroup. Metamorphic temperatures in the Hamersley Group nowhere exceeded ~ 300 °C and are often considerably lower. A slightly lower grade of bur- ial metamorphism at Paraburdoo is associated with relict primary haematite overgrown by magnetite in the BIFs, whereas elsewhere, e.g. at Mount Tom Price and Wittenoom, the meta- morphic grade is higher and replacement of pri- mary haematite by magnetite is essentially com- plete (Morris, 1985 ). This is evidence that most of the magnetite in the BIFs was produced dur- ing the burial metamorphism. Klein ( 1983 ) has discussed diagenesis and metamorphism of BIF, including the generation of magnetite as a late diagenetic/low-grade metamorphic mineral. Dales Gorge Member and the Joffre Member), the Weeli Wolli Formation and the Boolgeeda Iron Formation. The Wittenoom Dolomite occurs between the lowest two BIFs. The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The myriad of mineralogical and textural va- rieties present in the ores has been studied in de- tail by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ). The following brief summary of current ideas on the BIF to ore transformation is far from comprehensive and only serves to give the reader a flavour of the complex evolution recognized by Morris. Fol- lowing exposure of fresh BIF during a period of uplift and erosion, iron has been concentrated at depth by an electrochemical supergene process. This involved concentration by leaching of some gangue without replacement, as well as the me- tasomatic replacement of gangue (chert and car- bonates) by hydrous iron oxides, mostly goe- thite. The iron in this metasomatic goethite is derived from weathering of BIF up-dip from the zone of ore formation. Magnetite in the fresh BIF is converted to martite and cation-deficient magnetite, termed "kenomagnetite" by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ), during the ore-forming process. Anisotropy also causes cones of confidence to be underestimated, due to compression of the range of inclinations. In principle, deflection of post-folding remanence towards the bedding plane by high magnetic anisotropy can produce an ap- parent syn-folding signature, with best agreement between directions from different fold limbs after partial unfold- ing. Thus high anisotropy cannot only bias estimated palaeofield directions and cause underestimation of errors, but can also mislead interpretation of the time of remanence acquisition. The anisotropy of anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) probably yields an upper limit to the anisotropy of the chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) carried by the BIFs. Therefore, from the anisotropy of ARM, a maximum inclination deflection of 9 ° is suggested for the sampled BIFs. This corresponds to less than 5 ° change of palaeolatitude. The palaeomagnetic pole position calculated for BIFs at Paraburdoo is 40.9 ° S, 225.0 °E (dp = 2.9 °, drn = 5.8 ° ) after tilt correction, but without correction for anisotropy. Other pole positions reported include that from fiat- lying BIFs from Wittenoom at 36.4 ° S, 218.9 ° E (dp = 4.6 °, dm= 9.1 ° ), from Mount Tom Price iron ore at 37.4 ° S, 220.3°E (dp= 5.7 °, din= 11.3 ° ) and from Paraburdoo ore at 36.4 ° S, 209.9°E (dp= 4.7 °, din= 8.8 ° ). The Hamersley and Fortescue Groups were subjected to low-grade (lowermost prehnite- pumpellyite facies to lowermost greenschist fa- cies) metamorphism due to burial beneath >t 5 km of the Turee Creek Group (Smith et al., 1982), before the initial folding, uplift and par- tial erosion of the Mount Bruce Supergroup. Metamorphic temperatures in the Hamersley Group nowhere exceeded ~ 300 °C and are often considerably lower. A slightly lower grade of bur- ial metamorphism at Paraburdoo is associated with relict primary haematite overgrown by magnetite in the BIFs, whereas elsewhere, e.g. at Mount Tom Price and Wittenoom, the meta- morphic grade is higher and replacement of pri- mary haematite by magnetite is essentially com- plete (Morris, 1985 ). This is evidence that most of the magnetite in the BIFs was produced dur- ing the burial metamorphism. Klein ( 1983 ) has discussed diagenesis and metamorphism of BIF, including the generation of magnetite as a late diagenetic/low-grade metamorphic mineral. Applying the fold test of McFadden and Jones ( 1981 ), a common true mean direction for the Wittenoom and Par- aburdoo BIFs is rejected with more than 99% confidence before tilt correction, but cannot be rejected, even with only 86% confidence, after tilt-correction. This therefore constitutes a posi- tive fold test and indicates that the BIFs ac- quired their magnetization before folding. The fold test assumes, however, that the directions are Fisher distributed, which is not the case here be- cause the distribution of inclinations has been somewhat compressed by the anisotropy. In principle, therefore, the fold test is only qualita- tive. A knowledge of the remanent magnetization, the magnetic suscepti- bility and the anisotropy of magnetic suscepti- bility (AMS) of banded-iron formations (BIFs) and iron ores of the Hamersley Group was re- quired to assist in exploration. Dales Gorge Member and the Joffre Member), the Weeli Wolli Formation and the Boolgeeda Iron Formation. The Wittenoom Dolomite occurs between the lowest two BIFs. The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The myriad of mineralogical and textural va- rieties present in the ores has been studied in de- tail by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ). The following brief summary of current ideas on the BIF to ore transformation is far from comprehensive and only serves to give the reader a flavour of the complex evolution recognized by Morris. Fol- lowing exposure of fresh BIF during a period of uplift and erosion, iron has been concentrated at depth by an electrochemical supergene process. This involved concentration by leaching of some gangue without replacement, as well as the me- tasomatic replacement of gangue (chert and car- bonates) by hydrous iron oxides, mostly goe- thite. The iron in this metasomatic goethite is derived from weathering of BIF up-dip from the zone of ore formation. Magnetite in the fresh BIF is converted to martite and cation-deficient magnetite, termed "kenomagnetite" by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ), during the ore-forming process. Anisotropy also causes cones of confidence to be underestimated, due to compression of the range of inclinations. In principle, deflection of post-folding remanence towards the bedding plane by high magnetic anisotropy can produce an ap- parent syn-folding signature, with best agreement between directions from different fold limbs after partial unfold- ing. Thus high anisotropy cannot only bias estimated palaeofield directions and cause underestimation of errors, but can also mislead interpretation of the time of remanence acquisition. The anisotropy of anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) probably yields an upper limit to the anisotropy of the chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) carried by the BIFs. Therefore, from the anisotropy of ARM, a maximum inclination deflection of 9 ° is suggested for the sampled BIFs. This corresponds to less than 5 ° change of palaeolatitude. The palaeomagnetic pole position calculated for BIFs at Paraburdoo is 40.9 ° S, 225.0 °E (dp = 2.9 °, drn = 5.8 ° ) after tilt correction, but without correction for anisotropy. Other pole positions reported include that from fiat- lying BIFs from Wittenoom at 36.4 ° S, 218.9 ° E (dp = 4.6 °, dm= 9.1 ° ), from Mount Tom Price iron ore at 37.4 ° S, 220.3°E (dp= 5.7 °, din= 11.3 ° ) and from Paraburdoo ore at 36.4 ° S, 209.9°E (dp= 4.7 °, din= 8.8 ° ). The Hamersley and Fortescue Groups were subjected to low-grade (lowermost prehnite- pumpellyite facies to lowermost greenschist fa- cies) metamorphism due to burial beneath >t 5 km of the Turee Creek Group (Smith et al., 1982), before the initial folding, uplift and par- tial erosion of the Mount Bruce Supergroup. Metamorphic temperatures in the Hamersley Group nowhere exceeded ~ 300 °C and are often considerably lower. A slightly lower grade of bur- ial metamorphism at Paraburdoo is associated with relict primary haematite overgrown by magnetite in the BIFs, whereas elsewhere, e.g. at Mount Tom Price and Wittenoom, the meta- morphic grade is higher and replacement of pri- mary haematite by magnetite is essentially com- plete (Morris, 1985 ). This is evidence that most of the magnetite in the BIFs was produced dur- ing the burial metamorphism. Klein ( 1983 ) has discussed diagenesis and metamorphism of BIF, including the generation of magnetite as a late diagenetic/low-grade metamorphic mineral. It has been suggested that the change from the "anoxic" conditions conducive to BIF forma- tion, to those favouring supergene iron enrich- ment, was related to the oxygen content of the Precambrian atmosphere reaching a threshold level able to satisfy the various oxygen "sinks" (Cloud, 1983 ). section_candidates.excerpt: alaeolatitudes, but can lead to large errors in calculated palaeopoles for intermediate to moderately steep palaeolatitudes. Anisotropy also causes cones of confidence to be underestimated, due to compression of the range of inclinations. In principle, deflection of post-folding remanence towards the bedding plane by high magnetic anisotropy can produce an ap- parent syn-folding signature, with best agreement between directions from different fold limbs after partial unfold- ing. Thus high anisotropy cannot only bias estimated palaeofield directions and cause underestimation of errors, but can also mislead interpretation of the time of remanence acquisition. The anisotropy of anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) probably yields an upper limit to the anisotropy of the chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) carried by the BIFs. Therefore, from the anisotropy of ARM, a maximum inclination deflection of 9 ° is suggested for the sampled BIFs. This corresponds to less than 5 ° change of palaeolatitude. The palaeomagnetic pole position calculated for BIFs at Paraburdoo is 40.9 ° S, 225.0 °E (dp = 2.9 °, drn = 5.8 ° ) after tilt correction, but without correction for anisotropy. Other pole positions reported include that from fiat- lying BIFs from Wittenoom at 36.4 ° S, 218.9 ° E

Indian Peninsular shield is trellised by several generations of dolerite dikes, particularly in the granite-greenstone terrains (see Halls, 1982). Because they are so amenable to paleo- magnetic study, they are the source of the vast majority of Precambrian paleomagnetic data from India, especially from the Dharwar craton (Naqvi et al., 1974). Unfortunately, dolerite is difficult to date radiometrically, leaving the age of most Precambrian paleo-poles from India es- sentially unknown (Hargraves and Bhalla, 1983). Six samples (blocks or cores drilled in the field) were gathered at each of the twelve sites, and oriented with sun and magnetic compasses. Introduction The Indian Peninsular shield is trellised by several generations of dolerite dikes, particularly in the granite-greenstone terrains (see Halls, 1982). Because they are so amenable to paleo- magnetic study, they are the source of the vast majority of Precambrian paleomagnetic data from India, especially from the Dharwar craton (Naqvi et al., 1974). following paper is an abbreviated version of a thesis by Dawson (1984) which should be consulted for further details. 2. Sampling and laboratory procedure Five sites in each of the alkaline and dolerite swarms plus two sites in metadolerites were sam- pled for paleomagnetic study by Hargraves in 1981. Six samples (blocks or cores drilled in the field) were gathered at each of the twelve sites, and oriented with sun and magnetic compasses. NRM measurements were made with a Schon- stedt DSM-1 spinner magnetometer interfaced to an Apple IIe computer. Specimens were ther- mally demagnetized with a Schonstedt TSD-1 apparatus. The AF demagnetization equipment (maximum field 120 roT) rotates specimens around two perpendicular axes in an ambient DC field of less than 20 nT. All this equipment is housed in a magnetically shielded room. Demagnetization data were analyzed using Zijderveld vector diagrams (Dunlop, 1979) with linear regression (Kirschvink, 1980) and using the converging remagnetization circles tech- nique of Halls (1978). Vector means were cal- culated with both Fisher statistics and Bingham- Onstott statistics (Onstott, 1980), The remanent magnetism in the two metadol- erite dikes (sites 22, 23) was found to be ex- tremely weak and unstable. Hargraves Department of Geological and Geophysical Sciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Received June 15, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994 Abstract Thirteen (out of 16) oriented kimberlite samples from the Schuller and Franspoort pipes in the Premier swarm have yielded consistent stable remanent vectors after detailed AF demagnetization. The calculated poles (Schuller, n=8, 33.4°N, 53.5°E, ol95=6.0; Franspoort, n=5, 49.1 °N, 48.8°E, 0195=7.5) are similar to those previously de- termined for the Premier and National pipes. The four poles are somewhat streaked, but their mean: n = 4, 30.0 ° N, 52.5 ° E, 0193 = 16.3, is considered to be a better estimate of the pole position for the Kaapvaal Craton ~ 1200 Ma ago. 1. Introduction Kimberlite pipes usually occur in "swarms" in which individual bodies represent a series of dis- tin

ich individual bodies represent a series of dis- tinct, but evidently roughly coeval intrusions. Although poles determined in this study are compatible with the APW path determined by previous studies (McElhinny and McWiUiams, 1977; Hattingh, 1986a,b,c, 1989), they suggest a more complex APW path than the broad swathe previously indicated by these authors. Pauls Department of Geology, University of Pretoria, Pretoria 0002, South Africa Received June 7, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994 Abstract Palaeomagnetic data have been acquired from seventeen sampling sites in the northern Bushveld Complex, Transvaal, South Africa. Twelve sites are situated in the main zone in the Potgietersrus area, while the remaining five are in the upper zone in the Villa Nora area. Specimens were subjected to alternating field and thermal de- magnetization. Two mean directions were found. One direction represents the main z

r 100 km in length (Gain and Mostert, 1982) (Fig. 1 ). It is roughly trian- gular in outline and consists of a central felsic portion with an outer rim of basic to ultramafic rocks. Younger sedimentary cover obscures one side of the triangle and much of the centre. This limb is truncated in the south by the northeast- trending Zebedela fault that brings Karoo sedi- ments into juxtaposition with the layered mafic rocks. Quaternary and Waterberg sedimentary rocks overlay the Potgietersrus limb to the north. To the west of the limb, the roof rocks are ex- posed, and consist of a variety of acid rocks and metasediments. The Archaean granites which compose the floor are exposed to the east. Pauls Department of Geology, University of Pretoria, Pretoria 0002, South Africa Received June 7, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994 Abstract Palaeomagnetic data have been acquired from seventeen sampling sites in the northern Bushveld Complex, Transvaal, South Africa. Twelve sites are situated in the main zone in the Potgietersrus area, while the remaining five are in the upper zone in the Villa Nora area. Specimens were subjected to alternating field and thermal de- magnetization. Two mean directions were found. One direction represents the main z

r 100 km in length (Gain and Mostert, 1982) (Fig. 1 ). It is roughly trian- gular in outline and consists of a central felsic portion with an outer rim of basic to ultramafic rocks. Younger sedimentary cover obscures one side of the triangle and much of the centre. This limb is truncated in the south by the northeast- trending Zebedela fault that brings Karoo sedi- ments into juxtaposition with the layered mafic rocks. Quaternary and Waterberg sedimentary rocks overlay the Potgietersrus limb to the north. To the west of the limb, the roof rocks are ex- posed, and consist of a variety of acid rocks and metasediments. The Archaean granites which compose the floor are exposed to the east. If the remanences post-date this de- formation, the Gawler Block poles GR and GA would be consistent with IM. It is not clear, however, how the overprint re- manences in the Gawler Block were acquired, given that the K-Ar closure temperatures for biotite are 200-350°C (Layer et al., 1989), whereas the unblocking temperature spectra for GR have their major peaks at or near the Curie temperature of magnetite (Chamalaun and Dempsey, 1978 ). Theoretical models for single- domain thermoviscous remanence would pre- dict much lower unblocking temperatures (e.g., Pullaiah et al., 1975), and experimental evi- dence on multidomains appears to suggest that only the spectral tails would reach the Curie tem- perature (Worm et al., 1988 ). In this paper we present the results of a new palaeomagnetic study on the mafic intrusions of the Mount Isa Inlier of northern Australia, with particular emphasis on unmetamorphosed dykes. The Inlier contains numerous intrusions of dif- ferent ages on which only one, reconnaissance, palaeomagnetic study has been reported (Duff and Embleton, 1976). That study yielded, among other results, a 1116 Ma pole. The latter cur- rently provides one of the few dated constraints on the 1400-900 Ma segment of the Australian APWP, although it is based on directions from only two dykes. 2. Geology and geochronology The Proterozoic Mount Isa Inlier outcrops over an area of about 50,000 krn 2 (Fig. 1 ). Its major Precambrian neighbours are the McArthur Basin to the west and the Arunta Block to the south- west. The former is part of the North Australian Craton (Plumb, 1979) which extends from the western Mount Isa Inlier to the Kimberley Block. The latter, Arunta Block, together with the Mus- grave Block, is part of the system of Central Aus- tralian Mobile Belts (Plumb, 1979) which en- closes the Yilgarn and Pilbara Blocks (the West Australian Shield), and

Most proved unsuitable because of unstable reman- ences or highly scattered directions; none gave a fully satisfactory result. Diamond occurrences in India In 1980/81 oriented samples for paleomag- netic study were drilled from seven kimberlite or lamproite occurrences in south and central India (see Fig. 1 ). Previously published radiomet

(Table 1 ) suggest that they were all intruded in late Proter- ozoic time, and hence were roughly coeval with the Premier swarm in South Africa, for which paleomagnetic data had already been published (Jones, 1968; Hargraves and Onstott, 1980; see Doppelhammer and Hargraves, 1994). If good paleomagnetic data could be obtained from the Indian occurrences, and the ages could be re- fined, then the paleogeographic contiguity, or otherwise, of India with Africa at that time could be ascertained. John Bristow reports (pers. com- mun., 1985) an age of 1079 Ma obtained by U- Pb measurements on perovskite separated from a Muligiripalle sample collected in this study. Diamonds were known to occur in sandstones and conglomerates as well as in the modern river gravels of India perhaps as early as 800 B.C. In- dia was trading in diamonds at least as early as the 4th century B.C., but little is known about this early period of diamond mining as nothing was written about it until the jeweller Jean-Bap- tiste Tavernier visited the mines in the mid- 17th century. Introduction The Japanese Islands are characterized by a zonal distribution of the pre-Neogene geologic terrains (Fig. 1). While the trend of this zonal structure is parallel to the axis of the island arc in Southwest Japan, this structure is sharply bent at the central Japan, which is called the Kanto Syntaxis. Detailed timing of the formation of this bend has been a controversial since the last century. KOBAYASHI (1941) explained this bend in the Cretaceous deformation of central Japan by the existence of an obstacle in front of the southward migrating Japanese Islands. TATEIWA (1976) considered that this cusp was formed in the Cretaceous to Paleogene time. While MATSUDA (1978, 1984) also placed the time of this cusp formation in the pre-Miocene, NIITSUMA (1982) set forth that the subduction of the Philippine Sea Plate initiated at 6-7 Ma in the Late Miocene caused the bending ofthe zonal structure. Furthermore, HYODO and NIITSUMA (1986) explained this cusp formation as a result of the collision of the Tanzawa Block with central Japan at 5 Ma. Recently, TAKAHASHI and NOMURA (1989) determined the paleomagnetic direction of the Late Miocene diorite body, which is located on the east wing of the Kanto Syntaxis, concluding that the Kanto Syntaxis was formed in the Late Miocene or earlier. While the timing of this deformation is one of the most important problems to discuss the tectonic development of the Japanese Islands, the detailed rotational motion of the Kanto Syntaxis remains still unknown. The Uchiyama area is located on the east wing of the Kanto Syntaxis, where the Middle Miocene to Pliocene volcanic and intrusive rocks are widely distributed. In these series, the Yaekubo Formation is a good target for paleomagnetic study, because many fresh andesite lava are intercalated in this formation. Introduction Paleomagnetic studies on volcanic rocks have made many contributions for understanding the nature of the past geomagnetic field. Sediments and sedimentary rocks, on the other hand, are now widely studied to reveal more or less continuous aspects of the paleomagnetic field, such as time sequence of paleosecular variation and polarity reversals. Paleomagnetism of volcanic rocks, however, is still important due to the following reasons; 1) stability of the remanence is in general much higher than that of sediments, 2) the remanence represents spot reading of the past geomagnetic field which is free from any kind of averaging effect, 3) radiometric ages can be obtained from the rock unit studied, and 4) it is possible to obtain an absolute paleointensity because the acquisition process of thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) can be reproduced in a laboratory. Volcanism has been quite active in Japan during Neogene and Quaternary, and so volcanic products such as lavas and pyroclastic flows are widely distributed. Many paleomagnetic studies were carried out on these volcanic rocks (see, KINOSHITA,

SUNAKAWA (1988), the dataset is not quite large enough even for Brunhes chron. Moreover, paleointensity data from volcanic rocks in Japan are much fewer than paleodirection data (see, KONG, 1971; TANAKA, 1990). In this respect, paleosecular variation and paleointensity studies from volcanic rocks are still important especially for Brunhes and Matuyama chrons in which worldwide data can be compared owing to relatively large number of existing data. The purpose of this study is to obtain secular variation data in Brunhes and Matuyama from volcanic rocks of Zao Volcano Group which has been active during Pleistocene. All the rock units sampled in this study have radiometric ages obtained by K-Ar method and cover the time span between about 0.1 Ma and 1 Ma. The K-Ar dates were obtained by using a mass spectrometer which was specially made for the purpose of dating young rocks. Paleosecular variation study from such accurately dated volcanic rocks is very useful to discuss the fluctuation of the geomagnetic field in the time scale of 104 - 105 years. 2. Introduction Although the main purpose of paleomagnetism is to study the behavior of the Earth's magnetic field in the past, paleomagnetic information can also be used to constrain important volcanological aspects. In this paper, paleomagnetic results from eight, randomly selected, lava flows from the Azufre volcano, Andean Cordillera (35.25°S, 289.5°E) are reported. Due to the interbedding of lavas from two volcanoes (Azufre and Planchon, Fig. 1(a)), anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) measurements were made to determine flow directions of the sampled lavas. Additionally, magnetic correlation techniques were used 1) to test the hypothesis of rapid extrusion of lava flows, and 2) to constrain the age of the Azufre lavas by comparing their directions of magnetization with that obtained from a group of lavas of the Mendoza and Neuquen provinces, Argentina, which have been previously dated by radiometric methods. 2. Geological Setting and Sampling Procedures The site of study is located in a transition zone between andesite volcanoes to the north and basalt- dacite volcanoes to the south (TORMEY et al., 1989). The pole position from the Werrikimbe Volcanics is at 31.6° S, 185.3° E (A95 = 26.6°). These rocks are the volcanic expression of widespread igneous activity during the Late Triassic (~ 226 Ma). While this activity is an obvious potential cause of the magnetic overprinting found in the older units, the magnetic directions from the volcanics and the overprints are not coincident. However, because only a few units could be sampled, the error in the mean direction from the volcanics makes it difficult to make a fair comparison with the directions of overprinted units. Natural remanent magnetization and laboratory- induced remanences were measured using either a Can- adian Thin Film three-axis cryogenic magnetometer or an upgraded and modified fluxgate spinner magnet- ometer. The demagnetizers used were a Schonstedt AF demagnetizer model GSD-1 and the CSIRO three-stage carousel furnace. The furnace is housed inside a 4 m ten coil Helmholtz set with automatic feed-back maintaining zero-field (< 5 nT). These rocks are the volcanic expression of widespread igneous activity during the Late Triassic (~ 226 Ma). While this activity is an obvious potential cause of the magnetic overprinting found in the older units, the magnetic directions from the volcanics and the overprints are not coincident. However, because only a few units could be sampled, the error in the mean direction from the volcanics makes it difficult to make a fair comparison with the directions of overprinted units. The overprint poles determined from normal polarity magnetizations of the Kullatine Formation is at 61.0°S, 155.6°E (A95 = 6.9°) and a basalt from Ellenborough is at 50.7° S, 148.8° E (A95 = 15.4°), and from reversed polarity magnetizations, also from the basalt at Ellenborough is at 49.4° S, 146.2° E (A95 = 20.4°). These are closer to either an Early Permian or a mid- Cretaceous position, rather than a Late Triassic position, on the Australian apparent polar wandering path. Therefore, despite their mixed polarity, and global observations that the Permian and mid-Cretaceous geomagnetic fields were of constant polarities, the age of these overprint magnetizations appears to be either Early Permian or mid-Cretaceous. Units sampled from the Southern Hastings Terrane include the Late Devonian (?) basalt at Ellenborough, the Early Carboniferous Taree Limestone (Quintoc Group), the Early Permian Cedar Party Limestone (Manning Group) and serpentinites associated with the southwestern margin of the block. METHODS AND TECHNIQUES Routine palaeomagnetic methods (McElhinny 1973; Collinson 1983) were used throughout. All samples were subjected to alternating field and thermal demagnetiz- ation. Natural remanent magnetization and laboratory- induced remanences were measured using either a Can- adian Thin Film three-axis cryogenic magnetometer or an upgraded and modified fluxgate spinner magnet- ometer. The demagnetizers used were a Schonstedt AF demagnetizer model GSD-1 and the CSIRO three-stage carousel furnace. The furnace is housed inside a 4 m ten coil Helmholtz set with automatic feed-back maintaining zero-field (< 5 nT). Components of magnetization have been isolated using an interactive version of LINEFIND (Kent et al. 1983). The linear segments are fitted to data points weighted according to the inverse of their measured variances. This is typical for red-beds whose remanence is predominantly carried by hematite. At most sites directions of natural remanent magnetization from the Kullatine Formation were well grouped close to, or a little steeper than, the present field direction. However, at the two sites from near Kookaburra (Kul5 and Kul6) natural remanent magnetization directions were shallow to the northwest. These were the only sites where magnetizations with well grouped shallow directions were observed. These shallow components were removed by thermal cleaning to about 500° C, or more readily by an alternating field of about 40 mT. METHODS AND TECHNIQUES Routine palaeomagnetic methods (McElhinny 1973; Collinson 1983) were used throughout. All samples were subjected to alternating field and thermal demagnetiz- ation. Natural remanent magnetization and laboratory- induced remanences were measured using either a Can- adian Thin Film three-axis cryogenic magnetometer or an upgraded and modified fluxgate spinner magnet- ometer. The demagnetizers used were a Schonstedt AF demagnetizer model GSD-1 and the CSIRO three-stage carousel furnace. The furnace is housed inside a 4 m ten coil Helmholtz set with automatic feed-back maintaining zero-field (< 5 nT). Components of magnetization have been isolated using an interactive version of LINEFIND (Kent et al. 1983). Natural remanent magnetization and laboratory- induced remanences were measured using either a Can- adian Thin Film three-axis cryogenic magnetometer or an upgraded and modified fluxgate spinner magnet- ometer. The demagnetizers used were a Schonstedt AF demagnetizer model GSD-1 and the CSIRO three-stage carousel furnace. The furnace is housed inside a 4 m ten coil Helmholtz set with automatic feed-back maintaining zero-field (< 5 nT). Components of magnetization have been isolated using an interactive version of LINEFIND (Kent et al. 1983). All of the rest of the sam- ples responded well to A.F. cleaning, and all but one decayed to less than ten percent of initial intensity. This set has both a normal and a reversed component similar to the other sites, but the coercivities of the directions overlap completely. Seven samples only have the northerly and up direction in the range of 20 to 70 mT. Nine samples have the southerly and down direction in the similar range of 5 to 90 mT. Only one of the samples has both directions, a small normal component from 5 to 20 roT. Not only is the coercivity greater for these samples' normal components, but it also is rotated clockwise from the present day magnetic field. These two factors make the normal component from this site a prime candidate for being antipodal to the reversed field instead of being a secondary present day field com- ponent (see discussion section). The plutons record both a normal and a reversed characteristic direction. The mean normal direction has a declination of 3.4 °, an inclination of -38.5 °, and an alpha 95 of 10.5". The mean reversed direction has a declination of 207.8*, an inclination of 33.8", and an alpha 95 of 10.8". This general approach helped to locate and statistically define linear regions (i.e. individual magnetic components) of the data. By grouping common components from each sample within a site, mean directions were then calculated for each site according to standard paleomagnetic pro- cedures (Fisher, 1953). After determining the means and Fisherian parameters, including a precision parameter (k) and an accuracy estimation (alpha 95) for each site, the means were used to calculate average directions for the region as a whole. Paleopoles were calculated from the overall mean declinations and inclinations using the axial geocentric dipole hypothesis. INTRODUCTION THIS PAPER PRESENTS the results of a paleomagnetic investigation of Jurassic to Cretaceous plutons exposed in the Coastal Ranges of Northern Chile between latitudes of 24 ° to 25°S (Fig.l). It is the fourth paleomagnetic study done in the area, but it is the first to provide results from a regionally extensive sample suite within the Jurassic to Cretaceous coastal batholith. The objective was to further the understanding of the Mesozoic and Cenozoic tectonic development of the Coastal Cordillera. In recent years, a number of paleo- magnetic studies have revealed a complex pattern of post-Paleozoic rotations within the coastal province of Peru and Chile (for review see Beck, 1988; Forsythe et al., 1987). Some workers, in viewing these rotations, have invoked models of oroclinal bending (Heki et al., 1983, 1984; Kono etal., 1985; May and Butler, 1985) following ideas initially expressed by Carey (1955). Others have promoted models of more local

(1988), have been completed in the Antofagasta Province where the Coastal Ranges are separated from a longitudinal depression (Pampa de Taramugal) and the main cordilleran ranges by the Ata- cama Fault Zone. These studies all yielded data with discordant declinations, suggesting clockwise rotations up to-30 °, but had very restricted sampling areas covering a maximum diameter of-10 km. Because of the restricted sampling areas, it has been difficult to ascertain whether the inferred tectonic rotations at these sites are localized or representative of a more regional phenomena such as motion along, or related to, the Atacama Fault Zone. This study was designed to determine the regional extent and character of these inferred rotations. It was aided by the dating in recent years of a suite of the Jurassic and Cretaceous plutons, but is also hindered by the paucity of good outcrops and the general difficulty of access. The oldest unit, "Paleozoic Basement", is a generic name for a collection of plutonic and metamorphic rocks that represent various elements of the region's pre-Jurassic history (see Dalziel and For- sythe, 1985; Coira et al, 1982; Bahlburg et al., 1987). This basement is intruded by the "Mesozoic Coastal Batholith" which is composed of gabbros, granodiorites, granites, late-stage aplites, and various mafic to inter- mediate dike swarms (Garcia, 1967; Ferraris and DiBi- ase, 1978) that in the sampling area range in age from 128 to 157 Ma (Herv6 et al., 1985; see Table 1). INTRODUCTION THIS PAPER PRESENTS the results of a paleomagnetic investigation of Jurassic to Cretaceous plutons exposed in the Coastal Ranges of Northern Chile between latitudes of 24 ° to 25°S (Fig.l). It is the fourth paleomagnetic study done in the area, but it is the first to provide results from a regionally extensive sample suite within the Jurassic to Cretaceous coastal batholith. The objective was to further the understanding of the Mesozoic and Cenozoic tectonic development of the Coastal Cordillera. In recent years, a number of paleo- magnetic studies have revealed a complex pattern of post-Paleozoic rotations within the coastal province of Peru and Chile (for review see Beck, 1988; Forsythe et al., 1987). Some workers, in viewing these rotations, have invoked models of oroclinal bending (Heki et al., 1983, 1984; Kono etal., 1985; May and Butler, 1985) following ideas initially expressed by Carey (1955). Others have promoted models of more local

(1988), have been completed in the Antofagasta Province where the Coastal Ranges are separated from a longitudinal depression (Pampa de Taramugal) and the main cordilleran ranges by the Ata- cama Fault Zone. These studies all yielded data with discordant declinations, suggesting clockwise rotations up to-30 °, but had very restricted sampling areas covering a maximum diameter of-10 km. Because of the restricted sampling areas, it has been difficult to ascertain whether the inferred tectonic rotations at these sites are localized or representative of a more regional phenomena such as motion along, or related to, the Atacama Fault Zone. This study was designed to determine the regional extent and character of these inferred rotations. It was aided by the dating in recent years of a suite of the Jurassic and Cretaceous plutons, but is also hindered by the paucity of good outcrops and the general difficulty of access.
